unit.title: Perform advanced welding using flux cored arc welding process - FCAW

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Compare rutile (T-1) and basic (T-5) gas-shielded flux-cored wires with an all-position self-shielded wire such as E71T-8. Say which you would choose for three different jobs, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Rutile T-1 wires have a smooth spray-like arc, little spatter and a fast-freezing slag that holds the pool, so the all-position types suit vertical and overhead work. They give good-looking welds but more hydrogen and less toughness than basic wires. Basic T-5 wires have a lime-type slag that gives low hydrogen, very tough weld metal and good resistance to cracking, but the arc is more globular and the slag holds the pool less, so they are harder to use out of position. Self-shielded wires such as E71T-8 need no gas, so they suit windy sites; the T-8 type is all-position and gives good toughness, but makes more fume and needs the stick-out the maker gives. I would choose a T-1 wire for general shop work on frames in all positions, a T-5 wire for a thick, restrained crane girder joint, and a T-8 wire for a steel frame welded on an open site near the sea, each only where the WPS covers it.
markingPoints: T-1: smooth arc, slag holds pool, all-position; less tough
T-5: low hydrogen, tough, crack-resistant; harder out of position
T-8: no gas, site work, all-position, toughness; fume and stick-out
Gives three sensible jobs with reasons
Keeps to what the WPS covers

essays.stem: Explain what causes hydrogen cracking in thick FCAW welds, and describe how a welder and supervisor prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Hydrogen cracking needs three things together: hydrogen in the weld, a hard structure in the weld or heat-affected zone, and stress from restraint. Hydrogen comes from moisture in the wire flux, the gas, rust, oil or paint on the joint, and damp air. Thick or high-strength steel cools fast and can form a hard zone, and a big, stiff joint holds high stresses. The crack can appear hours after welding. To prevent it, we choose a low-hydrogen wire, such as one with an H4 or H8 mark, keep wire sealed and dry and do not use damp spools, and clean the joint to bright metal. We preheat to the WPS figure, including for tacks, and keep the interpass temperature in range so the joint cools slowly. Sometimes the WPS asks for the joint to be kept warm after welding. Because cracks may be delayed, final inspection of critical joints is done after a waiting time, often with magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing.
markingPoints: Names hydrogen, hard structure and stress as causes
Gives sources of hydrogen
Low-hydrogen wire, dry storage, clean joints
Preheat, interpass control, slow cooling
Delayed final inspection with a suitable test

essays.stem: Describe how you would weld a double-V full-penetration butt joint in 20 mm carbon steel plate in the 2G position with FCAW, including back gouging and distortion control.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the WPS for the groove angles, root face, gap, wire, gas, settings and preheat. I bevel both sides of the plate edges, clean to bright metal, fit the plates with the gap given and a slight pre-set, and tack them, preheating the tack areas if the WPS asks. I fix the plates upright so the weld runs level. On the first side, I weld the root and a few fill passes as stringers, laid from the bottom of the groove upward, with the gun tilted slightly up so the metal does not sag. I clean slag after every pass and stagger the starts and stops. Then I turn to the other side and back gouge by grinding or air carbon arc gouging until sound weld metal shows, and check the groove. I weld the second side, then go back to the first side, working in turn so the shrinkage balances and the plate stays flat. I check flatness during the job and inspect the finished weld.
markingPoints: Prepares, fits, pre-sets and tacks to the WPS, with preheat
2G technique: stringers from the bottom up, gun tilted up
Cleans every pass and staggers starts and stops
Back gouges to sound metal and checks it
Welds the sides in turn to balance distortion and checks flatness

essays.stem: Explain what lamellar tearing is, where it happens, why, and how it can be prevented on FCAW work.
essays.modelAnswer: Lamellar tearing is a crack inside a steel plate, running in steps parallel to the plate surface, just below a weld. It happens mostly in T-joints and corner joints in thick plate, where a large weld pulls on the plate through its thickness. Rolled plate can contain thin, flat layers of impurities, and when the weld shrinks it pulls these layers apart. Big welds, stiff joints and plate with many layers make it worse. To prevent it, the designer can change the joint so the weld does not pull through the plate's thickness, or choose plate made with a guaranteed through-thickness property. Thick plate can be checked by ultrasonic testing for layers before welding. The welder can butter the face of the plate first with a soft layer of weld metal, use the smallest weld the drawing allows, keep to the welding sequence, and use a low-hydrogen wire with preheat as the WPS says.
markingPoints: Defines lamellar tearing as a stepped crack inside the plate
Says where: T and corner joints in thick plate
Explains why: layers in plate pulled by shrinkage through the thickness
Design and plate choice, ultrasonic check of plate
Buttering, small welds, sequence, low-hydrogen wire and preheat

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan and weld a 12 mm multi-pass fillet weld in the 2F position with FCAW, from the first pass to the final checks.
essays.modelAnswer: A 12 mm fillet is too big for one pass, because the metal would sag onto the bottom plate and give uneven legs and poor fusion. I check the WPS for the wire, settings and number of passes, and plan the beads in layers. The first pass goes into the root, with the gun aimed at the corner. The next layer has two beads: the first on the bottom plate, overlapping about half of the root pass, and the second above it, against the upright plate. The third layer has three beads, again starting at the bottom plate and working up. I keep each bead straight and even, clean all slag after every bead, especially at the toes, and stagger starts and stops. I keep the interpass temperature within the WPS. At the end, I measure both legs and the throat with a fillet gauge, and look for undercut on the upright plate, overlap on the bottom plate and slag at the toes.
markingPoints: Explains why one big pass is wrong
Plans layers and bead order, starting at the bottom plate
Cleans slag after every bead and staggers starts and stops
Keeps interpass temperature within the WPS
Measures legs and throat and checks for typical faults

essays.stem: A crack is found in an FCAW fillet weld on a structural steel member. Describe how you would repair it so that the repair can be accepted.
essays.modelAnswer: I mark the crack and report it to the supervisor and inspector, and record it. I find out how long and deep it is, using magnetic particle or dye penetrant testing at each end. I check there is a WPS that covers the repair, and find the likely cause so it is not repeated, such as hydrogen, poor fusion or too small a weld. I drill a small hole at each end of the crack if the procedure asks, then remove the crack by grinding or gouging, with sloping ends, until sound metal is reached. I check the groove with magnetic particle or dye penetrant testing to prove the whole crack is gone. I preheat if the WPS says, then re-weld with the approved wire and settings, cleaning between passes. After the waiting time the WPS or specification gives, the repair is inspected again by eye and by the same test. I record the repair, the welder and the results.
markingPoints: Reports, marks and records the crack
Finds its extent and likely cause; checks a repair WPS
Removes it to sound metal and proves it is gone
Preheats and re-welds to the WPS
Re-inspects after the waiting time and records

essays.stem: Explain how FCAW is used for the fill and cap of a carbon steel pipe joint in the 5G position after a GTAW or GMAW root, and how the joint is inspected.
essays.modelAnswer: An open root with FCAW is hard to control and can trap slag inside, so the root is usually put in with GTAW or short-circuit GMAW, which give a clean, even root. A second pass of the same process is often added so the root is thick enough not to burn through when FCAW starts. I clean the root and check the inside. For the FCAW fill and cap, I use an all-position wire and the settings on the WPS. I weld each half uphill from just past the bottom to just past the top, changing the gun angle as I go round, so the pool is held up by the slag. I clean slag after every pass with a wire brush or needle scaler, paying attention to the toes, and stagger the starts and stops. The cap is laid evenly with no undercut. The joint is inspected by eye inside and out, and by radiography or ultrasonic testing if the specification asks.
markingPoints: Explains why the root is GTAW or GMAW
Adds enough root thickness before FCAW
Welds each half uphill with all-position wire and changing gun angle
Cleans slag after each pass and staggers starts and stops
Inspects visually inside and out, and by NDT if required

essays.stem: Explain how you would estimate the wire, arc time and labour time for 20 m of 10 mm FCAW fillet weld. Use a wire efficiency of 85%, a deposit rate of 3 kg of weld metal per hour of arc time and an operating factor of 35%.
essays.modelAnswer: First I work out the weld metal. A 10 mm fillet has a cross-section of about 10 × 10 ÷ 2 = 50 mm². In 1 m that is 50 000 mm³, or 50 cm³, which at 7.85 g per cm³ weighs about 0.39 kg. For 20 m, that is about 20 × 0.39 = 7.85 kg of weld metal. Only 85% of the wire becomes weld metal, so the wire needed is 7.85 ÷ 0.85, about 9.2 kg. I would order a little extra, for example one 15 kg spool. The arc time is the weld metal divided by the deposit rate: 7.85 ÷ 3 = about 2.6 hours. Welders do not weld all the time; they also fit, clean and move. With an operating factor of 35%, the labour time is 2.6 ÷ 0.35, about 7.5 hours. I would add time for set-up and inspection, and use these figures to price and plan the job.
markingPoints: Works out the cross-section and mass per metre correctly
Works out the total weld metal (about 7.85 kg)
Works out the wire using 85% (about 9.2 kg)
Works out the arc time (about 2.6 h)
Works out the labour using 35% (about 7.5 h) and uses it to plan

essays.stem: Explain how you would read the welding symbols on a structural steel drawing before planning FCAW work, and how the symbols guide what you do.
essays.modelAnswer: Each welding symbol has an arrow pointing to the joint and a reference line. A weld symbol below the line means the weld is on the arrow side; above the line, it is on the other side; on both sides, both are welded. The shape of the symbol shows the weld type: a triangle for a fillet, a V or bevel for a groove. The number to the left gives the size, such as the fillet leg, and numbers to the right give the length and pitch of intermittent welds. A small circle at the bend means weld all round, and a flag means a field weld, made on site. A tail may give the process or WPS number. From these, I list each weld's type, size, length and side, decide which welds are done in the shop and which on site, choose the WPS for each, work out the wire and time, and plan an order of welding that controls distortion.
markingPoints: Explains arrow, reference line and arrow side/other side
Recognises fillet and groove symbols
Reads size, length and pitch
Knows the all-round circle, field-weld flag and tail
Uses the symbols to plan WPS, materials, shop or site work and sequence

essays.stem: As team leader of an FCAW crew in a busy fabrication shop, describe how you would control weld quality from day to day.
essays.modelAnswer: At the start of each shift, I check the WPSs for the day's jobs are at the bays, and that each welder is qualified for the work. I check the machines, guns, liners, gas and extraction, and that the wire on each feeder is the class the WPS lists, dry and labelled. I make sure joints are fitted and cleaned correctly before welding, and that preheat is done where needed. On the first piece of each job, I check the settings at the arc and inspect the weld fully before the rest are made. During the day, I walk round, watch technique, check that slag is cleaned between passes and that settings stay inside the WPS, and stop work that does not meet it. I coach welders whose work shows faults, explaining the cause and the fix. I make sure each weld is recorded with the welder, the wire batch and the inspection result, and that faults are reported and repaired properly.
markingPoints: Checks WPSs and welder qualifications
Checks equipment and that consumables match the WPS
First-off check of settings and weld
In-process checks, stopping work outside the WPS, coaching
Keeps records and deals with faults properly

practical1.title: Double-V full-penetration FCAW butt in the 2G position on 16–20 mm plate with back gouging, plus a 10 mm multi-pass 2F fillet, with macro sections
practical1.brief: Your group is given a WPS for a double-V butt joint in 16–20 mm carbon steel plate in the 2G (horizontal) position, and a WPS for a 10 mm multi-pass fillet in the 2F position, both with gas-shielded flux-cored wire. As a group, plan the work on the job sheet: who fits, who welds which side and passes, who back gouges, and who records. Every member must weld part of the butt joint (at least two passes) and at least one layer of the fillet. Fit and tack the butt plates with the gap and pre-set the WPS gives. Weld the first side, back gouge the second side by grinding (or air carbon arc gouging, if the Centre allows it and the assessor supervises) to sound metal, then weld the sides in turn. Check flatness with a straight edge before and after. Weld the 10 mm fillet in layers, with bead order marked on a sketch first. The group then cuts one macro section from each joint, under supervision, etches it and measures the fillet legs and throat. Record settings, interpass temperatures and results on the record sheet. Photograph each stage below.
materials: 16–20 mm carbon steel plates, bevelled for a double-V, and plate for a tee joint
Gas-shielded all-position flux-cored wire (such as E71T-1 type, as the WPS lists) and shielding gas
FCAW sets with flowmeters, and a stand that holds plate in 2G
Grinder with grinding discs (and an air carbon arc gouging set only if the Centre allows it)
Needle scaler or power wire brush, chipping hammer, straight edge, fillet gauge, temperature crayons
Saw, abrasive papers and etching solution with its SDS (used under supervision)
WPSs, job sheet and record sheet (from the assessor)
photos: The job sheet with roles and the bead-order sketch
The fitted and tacked double-V with the straight edge showing the pre-set
The back-gouged root before the second side
The finished double-V on both faces and the finished 10 mm fillet
The two etched macro sections with the fillet gauge on the fillet
checklist: Helped plan the job and the bead order, and kept to his or her role
Welded at least two passes of the butt in 2G with no sagging or slag at the toes
Cleaned slag fully after each pass and staggered starts and stops
Back gouged to sound metal, or checked the gouge correctly
Laid fillet beads in the planned order, giving even legs
Recorded settings, interpass temperatures and results accurately
Worked safely with the grinder, gouging set and etchant
safety: Wear full PPE, with trousers over boot tops and a face shield over glasses when grinding or gouging
Use extraction at each bay; flux-cored fume contains manganese
Gouging only if the Centre allows it, with the assessor supervising, screens up and fire watch
Wear hearing protection with the needle scaler and grinder
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Multi-process carbon steel pipe joint: GTAW or GMAW root, then all-position FCAW fill and cap in the 5G position, with inspection and a macro
practical2.brief: Your group is given a WPS for a carbon steel pipe butt joint with a GTAW or short-circuit GMAW root (as the Centre's equipment allows) and an all-position FCAW fill and cap, in the 5G position (pipe fixed horizontal). Each member, or each pair if pipe is short, makes one joint. Roles rotate so that every member fits and tacks, puts in a root or second pass, and welds FCAW fill or cap passes on a joint. Prepare and check the bevels, root face and gap; tack; and fix the pipe in the stand. Weld the root and a second pass with GTAW or GMAW, clean and check the root from inside, then weld the FCAW passes uphill on each half, cleaning slag between passes and staggering starts and stops. One member records the processes, wires, settings and passes for each joint. Inspect each finished joint by eye, inside and out, and with a weld gauge. The assessor chooses one joint to be cut at the bottom (6 o'clock) and at one side; the group etches the faces and reports on fusion between the root and the FCAW passes. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Bevelled carbon steel pipe pieces, about 100–150 mm outside diameter, 6–8 mm wall
GTAW set with ER70S-2 rods, or GMAW set with solid wire, for the root
FCAW sets with all-position gas-shielded flux-cored wire and gas
Gap gauge, hi-lo gauge, mirror, weld gauge, needle scaler or power wire brush and grinder
Saw, abrasive papers and etching solution with its SDS (used under supervision)
WPS and blank record sheet (from the assessor)

checklist: Prepared, fitted and tacked the pipe to the WPS
Welded a root or second pass that was sound and thick enough for FCAW
Welded FCAW passes uphill with the gun angle changed round the pipe
Cleaned slag between passes and staggered starts and stops
Inspected a joint inside and out and recorded it correctly
Read the macro and reported on fusion between the processes
safety: Clamp the pipe stands firmly; keep hot pipe on the stand or in the cooling area, marked HOT
Wear full PPE, with a cap and closed collar for the overhead part of the pipe
Use extraction for both processes; keep argon and CO2 cylinders chained upright
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
